proof:
# Four monotone common-vertex triangle fibers have a sufficient own centroid

Let T={(x1,x2): x1,x2>=0, x1+x2<=1}, let V=|T|, and put
Gamma=4/9. Suppose the four actual integer fibers, at bases 0,1,2,3,
are r_k T, with positive concave radii

    0<r_0<=r_1<=r_2<=r_3.

Write M=V sum r_k^2 for their mixed mass, and let
A_mu(y)=inf_{closed halfspaces H containing y} mu(H) denote absolute
cap depth. Then one of the following two specified own-fiber
centroids has A_mu(y)>=Gamma M/2, or normalized depth at least 2/9:

* if r_3^2 >= (sum r_k^2)/2, use the centroid of the last fiber;
* otherwise use (2,(r_2/3,r_2/3)), the penultimate fiber's centroid.

The decreasing case follows by reversing the base. All cap normals,
all real base tilts, and closed vertical caps are included. This is a
four-fiber theorem; no arbitrary-chain centroid claim is made.

## 1. The exact positive-normal envelope of a triangle cap

Define the normalized envelope

    P_r(t)=min_{w1,w2>=0, w1+w2=1}
           |rT intersect {w1 x1+w2 x2>=t}|/V.

It is exactly

    r^2,                    t<=0;
    (r-t)^2,                0<=t<=r/3;
    4t(r-2t),               r/3<=t<=r/2;
    0,                      t>=r/2.                         (1)

Here all formulas agree at shared endpoints. For t>=r/2 the normal
(1/2,1/2) has zero-area cap. For the remaining proper case put
theta=t/r and, by coordinate symmetry, write w=(alpha,1-alpha),
1/2<=alpha<=1. The normalized cap fraction is

    1-theta^2/[alpha(1-alpha)],  theta<=1-alpha;
    (alpha-theta)^2/[alpha(2alpha-1)], theta>=1-alpha.       (2)

The first expression decreases up to its interface with the second.
The derivative of the second has the sign of

    alpha(4theta-1)-theta.

For theta<=1/3 it is minimized at alpha=1 and gives (1-theta)^2.
For 1/3<=theta<1/2 the minimizing alpha is

    alpha=theta/(4theta-1),

which belongs to [1-theta,1]; substitution gives
4theta(1-2theta). This proves (1), including the coordinate and
equal-normal limits. In particular

    P_r(t)>=Gamma r^2 whenever t<=r/3.                     (3)

Unlike independently minimizing opposite members of a reflected
pair, this envelope preserves one shared base tilt. It does relax
the common continuous normal, so its sum is a lower bound, not an
asserted exact mixed-depth formula.

## 2. A two-threshold inequality

For every 1/2<=b<=1 and 1/6<=x<=1/3,

    P_b(x)+P_1(2/3-x)>=Gamma b^2.                          (4)

In this interval, the second term is

    Q(x)=-8x^2+(20/3)x-8/9.

For fixed x consider P_b(x)-Gamma b^2 as a function of b.
For b<=2x it is -4b^2/9. For 2x<=b<=3x it is

    4xb-8x^2-4b^2/9,

a concave quadratic in b. For b>=3x it is nonnegative by (3).

If 1/6<=x<=1/4, the allowed b satisfy b>=1/2>=2x.
On the middle regime its minimum therefore occurs at b=1/2 or
b=3x. The latter contributes zero before adding Q(x), and the
former gives the exact sum

    Q(x)+P_(1/2)(x)-Gamma/4
       = (6x-1)(3-8x)/3 >=0.                              (5)

All regimes with b>=3x already give a nonnegative sum.
If 1/4<=x<=1/3, the minimum over every b>=0 of
P_b(x)-Gamma b^2 is -16x^2/9, attained at b=2x: this follows from
the monotonic first regime, concavity of the middle regime, and
nonnegativity of the last regime. Consequently the desired sum is
at least

    Q(x)-16x^2/9
       =4(11x-2)(1-2x)/9 >=0.                            (6)

This proves (4) for all real parameters, not just rational samples.

There is also a useful radius-growth bound. If d>=1 and
1/3<=t<=1/2, then

    P_d(t)-P_1(t)>=(2/3)(d^2-1)
                  >=(Gamma/2)(d^2-1).                   (7)

Indeed, along radii r>=1 the threshold satisfies t<=r/2. On
2t<=r<=3t the derivative of P_r(t) with respect to r is 4t>=4r/3;
on r>=3t it is 2(r-t)>=4r/3. The formulas agree at r=3t,
so integration proves (7). The letter d in (7) denotes a radius,
not a varying dimension; the geometric dimension remains two.

## 3. The three shared-tilt ranges

If the last fiber is heavy, its own ordinary centroid has cap mass
at least Gamma V r_3^2 >= Gamma M/2, so suppose it is not heavy.
Scale all radii and continuous coordinates by r_2. After this
common scaling write them as

    (a,b,1,d),   0<a<=b<=1<=d,
    d^2<a^2+b^2+1.                                       (8)

Concavity gives 2b>=a+1, in particular b>=1/2.
The chosen point is (2,(1/3,1/3)).

The exact positive-normal reduction in
`candidate 42889f299dc055c9` replaces any
cap through this own centroid by one actual ambient cap with
continuous normal w in the positive probability simplex and no
larger mass on any source fiber. Its four thresholds are

    1/3+2 beta,  1/3+beta,  1/3,  1/3-beta.               (9)

Thus its actual mass, divided by V, is at least the sum of the
four envelopes (1) at those thresholds. We verify the target
(Gamma/2)(a^2+b^2+1+d^2) for every real beta.

If beta>=0, the last threshold is at most 1/3<=d/3. The own and
last fibers alone contribute at least Gamma(1+d^2), which reaches
the target because a^2+b^2<=1+d^2.

If beta<=-1/6, the first fiber is captured in full. The second
threshold is at most 1/6<=b/3. The first three fibers therefore
contribute at least

    a^2+Gamma b^2+Gamma
       >= Gamma(a^2+b^2+1)
       > (Gamma/2)(a^2+b^2+1+d^2),                        (10)

where the last inequality uses the nonheavy assumption in (8).
No assertion that the complementary cap contains the old source
or any independently chosen subbody is used.

Finally let -1/6<=beta<=0 and put x=1/3+beta. The second and last
thresholds are x and 2/3-x. Equations (4) and (7) give the total
payment, even after discarding the first fiber,

    Gamma + P_b(x)+P_d(2/3-x)
       >= Gamma+Gamma b^2+(Gamma/2)(d^2-1)
       = (Gamma/2)(1+2b^2+d^2)
       >= (Gamma/2)(a^2+b^2+1+d^2).                       (11)

The last inequality is a<=b. Equations (10)--(11) and the first
tilt range cover all real tilts with no gap or limiting exception.

## 4. Geometry, boundary cases, and scope

Positive concavity of the radii makes the piecewise-linear roof
r(z) concave. Therefore the actual body

    {0<=z<=3, x1,x2>=0, x1+x2<=r(z)}

is convex, full-dimensional, and is the convex hull of its four
lifted integer fibers. The chosen centroid belongs to its positive
own fiber. The positive-normal reduction has a finite replacement
also for a purely base-normal closed cap: it retains or decreases
the mass of every whole boundary fiber. Thus vertical boundaries
are not discarded as null, and (9) suffices for them as well.

The endpoint-heavy case uses only its own fiber and includes
equality in the heavy condition. The proof therefore covers every
positive nondecreasing concave radius profile with four fibers,
including repeated radii and zero differences. Reflection of the
base gives the nonincreasing case. It also applies after a common
invertible continuous linear change or a common vertex shear that
is affine in the integer base.

For example, radii (2,3,4,5) have sum of squares 54, with no heavy
fiber. The theorem certifies the centroid at base 2 against every
cap with mass at least 12V. Its proof does not require the false
claim that coordinate or all-equal continuous normals suffice.

This proves neither the remaining four-fiber profiles with a strict
interior radius peak nor an arbitrary-length centroid selection
theorem. The standard-library verifier is
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_four_monotone_triangle_centroids.py`.
